summary: The target architecture splits 92 table mappings across five purpose-built engines: Aurora PostgreSQL owns 40% of the workload covering transactional writes and anything that needs strong consistency and ad-hoc queries, ElastiCache handles the high-frequency user lookups and API key reads at 121 and 98 requests per second respectively, DynamoDB covers 12 tables across 25 access patterns for the scheduler and key-value workloads, DocumentDB manages 87 document collections across 20 access patterns for the forum content layer, and OpenSearch handles 5 indexes for full-text search fed from DocumentDB via zero-ETL replication in near real-time. The biggest shift your team will feel is that JOINs no longer happen at the database layer: operations that previously joined users, posts, topics, and notifications in a single atomic transaction now use application-level orchestration, which means your engineers own the sequencing, and a handful of pre-computation jobs (permissions, topic scoring, webhook status) run on a schedule instead of at query time. Search results will trail writes by a few seconds, which is normal for this pattern and invisible to most users. This is a high-complexity migration and we designed for that: every access pattern is mapped, every capability gap has a schema-level solution, and the path forward is clear.
summary_deterministic: Analyzed 311 source tables and 1654 query patterns across 5 target database(s). Workload split: elasticache handles 487 queries (29.4%), aurora_postgresql handles 660 queries (39.9%), dynamodb handles 177 queries (10.7%), documentdb handles 229 queries (13.8%), opensearch handles 101 queries (6.1%). 92 source tables mapped across 3 engine(s). 92 source tables mapped to dynamodb, documentdb, opensearch. Estimated monthly cost: $814.12. 28 risk(s) identified (overall: HIGH). Top query groups by throughput: User lookups, API key management, Scheduler stats writes. Other targets evaluated: aurora_postgresql (67%), dynamodb (62%), documentdb (56%), opensearch (2%).

risks.description: [documentdb] Queries joining 3+ tables at high frequency. DocumentDB $lookup only supports simple equality (no correlated subqueries). Real-world: 4-7 table JOINs caused 72% I/O wait. (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 114 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Pre-denormalize via Extended Reference Pattern or write-time aggregation. Never chain $lookup operations.

risks.description: [documentdb] Queries with NOT IN, <>, !=, NOT EXISTS. These map to $ne/$nin/$nor which cause full collection scans in DocumentDB (no index usage). (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 3 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Redesign hot query paths to use positive equality operators ($eq, $in).

risks.description: [documentdb] Multi-dimensional analytics queries. $facet is NOT supported in any DocumentDB version. (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 74 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Run multiple aggregation pipelines in parallel at application layer.

risks.description: [documentdb] SQL window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, running totals). $setWindowFields is NOT supported in any DocumentDB version. (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 21 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Use Computed Pattern (pre-calculated fields) or application-layer computation.

risks.description: [documentdb] Queries with correlated subqueries. DocumentDB $lookup does NOT support let/pipeline syntax for correlated joins. Must be pre-denormalized. (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 159 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Pre-denormalize at write time. Use Extended Reference Pattern to embed frequently co-accessed fields.

risks.description: [documentdb] Self-referential FKs or recursive queries. $graphLookup is NOT supported in any DocumentDB version (including 8.0). (0% of queries resolved by schema design, 1 remaining)
risks.mitigation: Use Materialized Path pattern (store ancestor path as string), or pre-flatten hierarchies at write time. Consider Neptune for true graph workloads.

trade_offs.description: All FK relationships use reference strategy preserving independent write scalability at the cost of requiring application-level joins.
trade_offs.impact: Your application code must handle what PostgreSQL JOINs did automatically. Most reads that previously joined 2 tables (e.g., users + group_users) now require two separate queries. This adds 1-3ms per additional read but keeps write performance predictable and avoids unbounded document growth.

trade_offs.description: Category permission checks redesigned from NOT IN subquery to pre-computed user_accessible_categories collection maintained via Change Streams.
trade_offs.impact: Instead of computing permissions at query time with a NOT IN subquery, the system now pre-computes accessible category IDs per user and stores them in a dedicated collection. This shifts work from read time to write time. Category permission changes (rare) trigger recomputation; category lookups (frequent at 1.92 RPS design) become simple $in queries against pre-computed arrays.

trade_offs.description: Multi-table JOINs for webhook redelivery (3 tables) require application-layer orchestration since DocumentDB $lookup only supports simple equality.
trade_offs.impact: The webhook redelivery query joining redelivering_webhook_events to web_hook_events to web_hooks becomes multiple queries in application code. Consider storing webhook status directly on the redelivering event document via denormalization at write time.

trade_offs.description: Window functions (NTILE, ROW_NUMBER) used in top_topics scoring and badge queries are not supported in DocumentDB and require pre-computation.
trade_offs.impact: Topic scoring that uses NTILE() to compute percentile buckets must be pre-calculated by a background job and stored as a field on the document. This adds a scheduled job but eliminates real-time computation overhead entirely.

trade_offs.description: Loss of multi-document ACID transactions for operations spanning users, posts, topics, and notifications.
trade_offs.impact: Operations that previously modified multiple tables atomically (e.g., creating a post updates posts, topics, user_stats, notifications) must use application-level saga patterns or accept eventual consistency. For most forum operations, eventual consistency within 100ms is acceptable.

trade_offs.description: topic_voting_topic_vote_count is queried with many IN-list sizes (2-30+ topic IDs) all served by single index on topic_id.
trade_offs.impact: These batch lookups translate directly to $in queries which DocumentDB handles efficiently with a single index. No design change needed, but monitor for IN-lists exceeding 1000 items which may cause performance degradation.

trade_offs.description: web_hooks collection denormalizes event_type_ids array from the join table web_hook_event_types_hooks to enable single-document lookups instead of 3-table JOINs.
trade_offs.impact: When webhook event type associations change, both the web_hooks document (event_type_ids array) and the web_hook_event_types_hooks collection must be updated. This is a bounded array (typically <20 event types) so no growth risk. Eliminates the need for $lookup chains at read time.

trade_offs.description: Users table uses GSI with ALL projection on username_lower to serve the highest-frequency lookup without a GetItem round-trip. The GSI is naturally sparse — only PROFILE entity items have username_lower.
trade_offs.impact: Every user profile write also writes to the GSI. At 53 users with infrequent mutations, the write amplification cost is negligible. The trade-off delivers sub-10ms username lookups without a second request.

trade_offs.description: Posts use PK=topic_id (N) and SK=post_number (N), enabling native range queries within a topic. PostsById GSI provides direct post_id lookups. PostsByTopicSortOrder GSI supports ordering by sort_order when it diverges from post_number.
trade_offs.impact: Direct lookup by post_id requires a GSI hop + GetItem. The PK+SK design enables COUNT and MAX patterns natively via Query (Select=COUNT, ScanIndexForward=false), eliminating the need for materialized counters at this scale.

trade_offs.description: Scheduler stats are modeled as a time-series with composite PK name#hostname and sort key started_at, enabling range queries by job execution time.
trade_offs.impact: The original auto-increment id is stored as an attribute but not used as a key. Updates require knowing name+hostname+started_at. The application must pass these values on the update path instead of just the id.

trade_offs.description: Users, UserEmails, UserOptions, and UserStats merged into a single Users table with PK=user_id and SK as entity type discriminator (PROFILE, EMAIL#<id>, OPTIONS, STATS).
trade_offs.impact: Reduces operational overhead from 4 tables to 1. Enables composite profile fetches in a single Query (PK=user_id). Trade-off: all user entities share capacity and backup settings. At 53 users this is strictly beneficial — shared monitoring, single IAM policy, single backup config.

trade_offs.description: Uniqueness for users.username is enforced via the UsersByUsername GSI partition key. The unique constraint on users.secure_identifier is enforced at the application layer.
trade_offs.impact: If two concurrent requests attempt to create users with the same username, the GSI will contain both items (GSIs don't enforce uniqueness). A conditional PutItem with attribute_not_exists on the base table, or a pre-check query on the GSI, is required. For this low-write-volume table (53 users), application-layer uniqueness is sufficient.

At 728 items with an INCLUDE projection (5 attributes), write amplification cost is negligible at this scale. If sort_order divergence from post_number is rare in this Discourse instance, consider removing this GSI and handling the edge case with a client-side sort on the base table Query results.

Monitor post-per-topic growth; if topics routinely exceed 100 posts, consider a materialized non_deleted_count attribute maintained via conditional UpdateItem on post create/delete.

trade_offs.description: Denormalized user profiles cached separately from full user rows - only the 9 most-queried columns are cached, not the full 37+ columns
trade_offs.impact: Reduces memory footprint by ~70% per user key but means admin-specific queries (e.g., checking suspended_till, silenced_till) still hit the database. This is acceptable since admin queries are low-frequency.

trade_offs.description: TTL-based staleness accepted for notifications (120s window) instead of real-time invalidation. List capped at 30 entries matching source query LIMIT.
trade_offs.impact: Users may see notifications up to 2 minutes late in Redis cache. This avoids complex pub/sub invalidation on every INSERT to the notifications table, which would add write amplification. For a forum, 2-minute delay is acceptable. 30-entry cap ensures bounded memory per user.

trade_offs.description: API key cache excludes last_used_at field and only invalidates on revocation rather than writing through on every request
trade_offs.impact: Eliminates ~11,770 unnecessary Redis HSET writes/hour for a non-functional timestamp. Revoked keys are still immediately invalidated via DEL. The last_used_at field continues to be updated in PostgreSQL only, which is acceptable since it is used for reporting, not auth decisions.

trade_offs.description: Topics+Categories JOIN pre-resolved at application layer using separate category cache rather than caching full JOIN results
trade_offs.impact: Instead of caching each unique topic query result (which has many variants), we cache categories as reference data and let the application resolve the JOIN. This reduces key explosion (dozens of query variants to 1 categories key + individual topic caches) but requires application-layer logic to filter by category permissions. categories:all is a potential hot key at scale - mitigate with RESP3 client tracking or local in-process cache.

trade_offs.description: Post content cached with 900s TTL - accepting potential stale like_count and read counts
trade_offs.impact: Like counts and read counts update frequently but the 900s TTL means displayed counts may lag. For a forum this is acceptable UX. The alternative (invalidating on every like) would generate excessive cache churn for the ~728 cached post keys.

trade_offs.description: Dual-key auth token storage (primary + prev) doubles Redis memory for session data but eliminates DB fallback during rotation window
trade_offs.impact: Each active session consumes two Redis keys (~768 bytes total) instead of one. At 500 active sessions this adds ~375KB - negligible. The benefit is that token rotation (a security-critical operation) never falls through to PostgreSQL, maintaining sub-ms session validation even during the rotation window.

trade_offs.description: Password hashes intentionally NOT cached in Redis - authentication always hits PostgreSQL
trade_offs.impact: At ~204 lookups/hour (~3.4/min), the DB load from password verification is minimal. Keeping credentials exclusively in PostgreSQL maintains stronger access controls, encryption-at-rest guarantees, and audit trails. The security risk of exposing password hashes in Redis (weaker ACLs, SSRF exposure, no row-level security) far outweighs the marginal latency savings.

A cache.t3.micro (0.5GB) would suffice, though a cache.t3.small or cache.m6g.large is recommended for operational headroom.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Complex multi-table JOINs between topics and categories with dynamic filtering (deleted_at IS NULL, visible, archetype, category_id IN) and varied ORDER BY clauses produce too many query variants to cache directly. The topic listing queries have dozens of variants that would require per-user, per-filter cache keys leading to excessive memory usage and low hit rates.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Cache categories as reference data (categories:all) and individual hot topics. Let the application resolve category JOINs in-memory. For the full topic listing, keep in PostgreSQL with proper indexing.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Analytical aggregation queries (COUNT with FILTER by date intervals for year/month/week/day stats) are not suitable for Redis. These compute rolling time-window aggregations across large datasets.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Pre-compute these stats on a schedule (e.g., every 5 minutes) and store the result in a Redis hash like stats:categories:{id}:post_counts with fields year, month, week, day. Or keep in PostgreSQL with materialized views.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Batch UPDATE statements that compute post scores using complex formulas (COALESCE with multiple columns, JOINs to topics) are write operations that cannot be served by Redis directly.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Continue executing these in PostgreSQL. After completion, invalidate affected post cache keys (posts:{post_id}) if the score change is significant enough to warrant cache refresh.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Password verification queries must remain in PostgreSQL for security. Caching credential material in Redis expands the attack surface unacceptably. Redis lacks row-level security, has weaker audit logging, and is more susceptible to SSRF-based exfiltration.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Keep password lookups in PostgreSQL. At ~204 calls/hour, this is not a performance bottleneck. Optimize with connection pooling if needed.

migration_notes.application_logic_required: Application must check revoked_at IS NULL after retrieving from Redis cache. If the key is found in cache but revoked_at is set, treat as invalid and DEL the cache key. last_used_at updates should be written to PostgreSQL only (not Redis) to avoid write amplification.

Sorted set uses sort_order as score and post_id as member. On cache miss, query posts with ORDER BY sort_order ASC and ZADD all pairs. Pagination via ZRANGE 0 19 (page 1), ZRANGE 20 39 (page 2), etc. On post delete: ZREM post_id. On new post: ZADD sort_order post_id.

The source query LEFT JOINs notifications with topics to filter out notifications for deleted topics. In Redis, store only notifications where topic is not deleted. On cache miss, rebuild from DB with WHERE (topics.id IS NULL OR topics.deleted_at IS NULL) ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 30.

Many queries fetch users with IN ($1, $2, ...$N) for N=2-35. Application should pipeline individual HMGET commands for each user_id, collecting results. On cache miss for any user, fetch from DB and populate Redis. Use MGET-style pipeline pattern.

Token rotation must use the Lua script (EC-AP-10) to atomically: 1) write new token data to user_auth_tokens:{new_auth_token}, 2) write same data to user_auth_tokens_prev:{new_prev_auth_token}, 3) DEL old primary and prev keys. On logout, DEL both keys for the session. Application must check rotated_at > threshold after cache hit to validate token freshness.

trade_offs.description: Posts and post_search_data are denormalized into a single 'discourse-posts' index, eliminating the need for cross-index joins that OpenSearch cannot perform.
trade_offs.impact: Application code that previously relied on a JOIN between posts and post_search_data tables no longer needs that logic — both are stored together. However, updates to search data require reindexing the entire document. This is a standard search-engine trade-off: read performance improves at the cost of slightly more complex write pipelines.

trade_offs.description: All indexes use 1 primary shard because the combined dataset is under 5MB total. The multi-node shard distribution rule is waived per the small-dataset exception.
trade_offs.impact: With only ~1,650 posts and 400 topics, the entire dataset fits comfortably in a single shard. This minimizes cluster overhead (fewer shard files, less coordination). As data grows past 20GB per index, shards should be increased — but at 10x growth multiplier the projected size is still well under 50MB, so 1 shard remains appropriate for the foreseeable future.

trade_offs.description: Topic title field uses multi_field mapping (text + keyword) to support both full-text search and exact-match/sorting use cases.
trade_offs.impact: The title field can be searched with relevance ranking (text subfield) and also used for exact duplicate detection (keyword subfield with case_insensitive). This doubles storage for that field but enables the case-insensitive LOWER(title) = LOWER($2) pattern without a custom normalizer.

trade_offs.description: Write operations (UPDATE, INSERT, UPSERT) remain in PostgreSQL. OpenSearch serves as a read-optimized search layer synced via CDC or application events.
trade_offs.impact: Teams must maintain a data synchronization pipeline between PostgreSQL (source of truth) and OpenSearch (search replica). Updates to posts, topics, or categories in PostgreSQL must be propagated to OpenSearch indexes. This adds operational complexity but is the standard pattern for search-optimized architectures.

trade_offs.description: English-language analyzer chosen for post raw_data and raw_data fields based on Discourse's use of PostgreSQL tsvector with English stemming configuration.
trade_offs.impact: The english_search custom analyzer provides stemming and stop-word removal, matching the behavior of PostgreSQL's to_tsvector('english', ...) that Discourse uses for search. Non-English content will still be indexed but may have reduced recall for stemmed queries. For multi-language deployments, consider per-locale index routing.

trade_offs.description: [PE note] [CAPACITY] Total dataset is ~5MB across all indexes. At this scale, a single 3-node cluster with 1 shard per index and 1 replica is well-provisioned. Monitor for growth past 1GB before reconsidering shard strategy.
trade_offs.impact: [CAPACITY] Total dataset is ~5MB across all indexes. At this scale, a single 3-node cluster with 1 shard per index and 1 replica is well-provisioned. Monitor for growth past 1GB before reconsidering shard strategy.

unsupported_patterns.source_query:
UPDATE topics
SET highest_staff_post_number = $1 + $2,
    highest_post_number = $3 + $4
    
    , posts_count = posts_count + $5
WHERE id = $6
RETURNING highest_post_number
unsupported_patterns.reason: OpenSearch does not support transactional UPDATE with atomic counter increments and RETURNING clause. This is a write-modify pattern that requires read-after-write consistency.
unsupported_patterns.recommendation: Keep this write pattern in the relational database (PostgreSQL). OpenSearch indexes should be updated asynchronously via CDC (Change Data Capture) or application-level sync after the authoritative write succeeds.

unsupported_patterns.source_query: INSERT INTO "post_search_data" ("raw_data","post_id","locale","version","search_data","private_message") VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6) ON CONFLICT ("post_id") DO UPDATE SET "raw_data"=excluded."raw_data","locale"=excluded."locale","version"=excluded."version","search_data"=excluded."search_data","private_message"=excluded."private_message" RETURNING "post_id"
unsupported_patterns.reason: OpenSearch does not support SQL UPSERT (INSERT ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE) with RETURNING semantics. However, OpenSearch _index API with document ID achieves similar insert-or-replace behavior.
unsupported_patterns.recommendation: Use OpenSearch index API with explicit _id set to post_id. The document will be created or fully replaced. Map this as a bulk_index operation in the sync pipeline.

unsupported_patterns.source_query:
UPDATE post_search_data
SET version = $1
FROM posts
WHERE post_search_data.post_id = posts.id
AND posts.topic_id = $2
unsupported_patterns.reason: Multi-table UPDATE with JOIN (UPDATE ... FROM ... WHERE) cannot be executed in OpenSearch. This requires cross-index coordination that OpenSearch does not support.
unsupported_patterns.recommendation: Keep this batch update in PostgreSQL. After execution, trigger a reindex of affected documents in the discourse-posts OpenSearch index via application logic or CDC.

unsupported_patterns.source_query:
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM (
  SELECT user_id
    FROM posts
   WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
     AND NOT hidden
     AND topic_id = $1
   ORDER BY post_number DESC
   LIMIT $2
) c
WHERE c.user_id = $3
unsupported_patterns.reason: Subquery with ORDER BY + LIMIT on inner query followed by outer COUNT with filter requires correlated subquery logic. OpenSearch does not support this pattern directly.
unsupported_patterns.recommendation: Implement in application layer: first query OpenSearch for the last N posts in a topic sorted by post_number desc, then filter client-side by user_id and count.

trade_offs.description: All FK relationships use reference strategy preserving independent write scalability at the cost of requiring application-level joins.
trade_offs.impact: Your application code must handle what PostgreSQL JOINs did automatically. Most reads that previously joined 2 tables (e.g., users + group_users) now require two separate queries. This adds 1-3ms per additional read but keeps write performance predictable and avoids unbounded document growth.

trade_offs.description: Category permission checks redesigned from NOT IN subquery to pre-computed user_accessible_categories collection maintained via Change Streams.
trade_offs.impact: Instead of computing permissions at query time with a NOT IN subquery, the system now pre-computes accessible category IDs per user and stores them in a dedicated collection. This shifts work from read time to write time. Category permission changes (rare) trigger recomputation; category lookups (frequent at 1.92 RPS design) become simple $in queries against pre-computed arrays.

trade_offs.description: Multi-table JOINs for webhook redelivery (3 tables) require application-layer orchestration since DocumentDB $lookup only supports simple equality.
trade_offs.impact: The webhook redelivery query joining redelivering_webhook_events to web_hook_events to web_hooks becomes multiple queries in application code. Consider storing webhook status directly on the redelivering event document via denormalization at write time.

trade_offs.description: Window functions (NTILE, ROW_NUMBER) used in top_topics scoring and badge queries are not supported in DocumentDB and require pre-computation.
trade_offs.impact: Topic scoring that uses NTILE() to compute percentile buckets must be pre-calculated by a background job and stored as a field on the document. This adds a scheduled job but eliminates real-time computation overhead entirely.

trade_offs.description: Loss of multi-document ACID transactions for operations spanning users, posts, topics, and notifications.
trade_offs.impact: Operations that previously modified multiple tables atomically (e.g., creating a post updates posts, topics, user_stats, notifications) must use application-level saga patterns or accept eventual consistency. For most forum operations, eventual consistency within 100ms is acceptable.

trade_offs.description: topic_voting_topic_vote_count is queried with many IN-list sizes (2-30+ topic IDs) all served by single index on topic_id.
trade_offs.impact: These batch lookups translate directly to $in queries which DocumentDB handles efficiently with a single index. No design change needed, but monitor for IN-lists exceeding 1000 items which may cause performance degradation.

trade_offs.description: web_hooks collection denormalizes event_type_ids array from the join table web_hook_event_types_hooks to enable single-document lookups instead of 3-table JOINs.
trade_offs.impact: When webhook event type associations change, both the web_hooks document (event_type_ids array) and the web_hook_event_types_hooks collection must be updated. This is a bounded array (typically <20 event types) so no growth risk. Eliminates the need for $lookup chains at read time.

trade_offs.description: Denormalized user profiles cached separately from full user rows - only the 9 most-queried columns are cached, not the full 37+ columns
trade_offs.impact: Reduces memory footprint by ~70% per user key but means admin-specific queries (e.g., checking suspended_till, silenced_till) still hit the database. This is acceptable since admin queries are low-frequency.

trade_offs.description: TTL-based staleness accepted for notifications (120s window) instead of real-time invalidation. List capped at 30 entries matching source query LIMIT.
trade_offs.impact: Users may see notifications up to 2 minutes late in Redis cache. This avoids complex pub/sub invalidation on every INSERT to the notifications table, which would add write amplification. For a forum, 2-minute delay is acceptable. 30-entry cap ensures bounded memory per user.

trade_offs.description: API key cache excludes last_used_at field and only invalidates on revocation rather than writing through on every request
trade_offs.impact: Eliminates ~11,770 unnecessary Redis HSET writes/hour for a non-functional timestamp. Revoked keys are still immediately invalidated via DEL. The last_used_at field continues to be updated in PostgreSQL only, which is acceptable since it is used for reporting, not auth decisions.

trade_offs.description: Topics+Categories JOIN pre-resolved at application layer using separate category cache rather than caching full JOIN results
trade_offs.impact: Instead of caching each unique topic query result (which has many variants), we cache categories as reference data and let the application resolve the JOIN. This reduces key explosion (dozens of query variants to 1 categories key + individual topic caches) but requires application-layer logic to filter by category permissions. categories:all is a potential hot key at scale - mitigate with RESP3 client tracking or local in-process cache.

trade_offs.description: Post content cached with 900s TTL - accepting potential stale like_count and read counts
trade_offs.impact: Like counts and read counts update frequently but the 900s TTL means displayed counts may lag. For a forum this is acceptable UX. The alternative (invalidating on every like) would generate excessive cache churn for the ~728 cached post keys.

trade_offs.description: Dual-key auth token storage (primary + prev) doubles Redis memory for session data but eliminates DB fallback during rotation window
trade_offs.impact: Each active session consumes two Redis keys (~768 bytes total) instead of one. At 500 active sessions this adds ~375KB - negligible. The benefit is that token rotation (a security-critical operation) never falls through to PostgreSQL, maintaining sub-ms session validation even during the rotation window.

trade_offs.description: Password hashes intentionally NOT cached in Redis - authentication always hits PostgreSQL
trade_offs.impact: At ~204 lookups/hour (~3.4/min), the DB load from password verification is minimal. Keeping credentials exclusively in PostgreSQL maintains stronger access controls, encryption-at-rest guarantees, and audit trails. The security risk of exposing password hashes in Redis (weaker ACLs, SSRF exposure, no row-level security) far outweighs the marginal latency savings.

trade_offs.description: Posts and post_search_data are denormalized into a single 'discourse-posts' index, eliminating the need for cross-index joins that OpenSearch cannot perform.
trade_offs.impact: Application code that previously relied on a JOIN between posts and post_search_data tables no longer needs that logic — both are stored together. However, updates to search data require reindexing the entire document. This is a standard search-engine trade-off: read performance improves at the cost of slightly more complex write pipelines.

trade_offs.description: All indexes use 1 primary shard because the combined dataset is under 5MB total. The multi-node shard distribution rule is waived per the small-dataset exception.
trade_offs.impact: With only ~1,650 posts and 400 topics, the entire dataset fits comfortably in a single shard. This minimizes cluster overhead (fewer shard files, less coordination). As data grows past 20GB per index, shards should be increased — but at 10x growth multiplier the projected size is still well under 50MB, so 1 shard remains appropriate for the foreseeable future.

trade_offs.description: Topic title field uses multi_field mapping (text + keyword) to support both full-text search and exact-match/sorting use cases.
trade_offs.impact: The title field can be searched with relevance ranking (text subfield) and also used for exact duplicate detection (keyword subfield with case_insensitive). This doubles storage for that field but enables the case-insensitive LOWER(title) = LOWER($2) pattern without a custom normalizer.

trade_offs.description: Write operations (UPDATE, INSERT, UPSERT) remain in PostgreSQL. OpenSearch serves as a read-optimized search layer synced via CDC or application events.
trade_offs.impact: Teams must maintain a data synchronization pipeline between PostgreSQL (source of truth) and OpenSearch (search replica). Updates to posts, topics, or categories in PostgreSQL must be propagated to OpenSearch indexes. This adds operational complexity but is the standard pattern for search-optimized architectures.

trade_offs.description: English-language analyzer chosen for post raw_data and raw_data fields based on Discourse's use of PostgreSQL tsvector with English stemming configuration.
trade_offs.impact: The english_search custom analyzer provides stemming and stop-word removal, matching the behavior of PostgreSQL's to_tsvector('english', ...) that Discourse uses for search. Non-English content will still be indexed but may have reduced recall for stemmed queries. For multi-language deployments, consider per-locale index routing.

trade_offs.description: [PE note] [CAPACITY] Total dataset is ~5MB across all indexes. At this scale, a single 3-node cluster with 1 shard per index and 1 replica is well-provisioned. Monitor for growth past 1GB before reconsidering shard strategy.
